source.title: The Quenching-Activation Behavior of the Gradient Descent Dynamics for Two-layer Neural Network Models
source.authors: Chao Ma; Lei Wu; E. Weinan

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper numerically studies gradient-descent training outcomes in two-layer networks across width, sample-size, initialization, and scaling regimes, using regression risks rather than classification error on benchmark datasets.
record.gate_note: Rows report the paper's own training-risk outcomes for conventional and mean-field GD. CIFAR benchmarks, classification error, corrupted labels, and the claim versions' other named studies are not tested. Results cited from prior work are not rows. Training-error curves shown only in figures are recorded as figure-only when the text does not provide their precise values.
record.test_reason: The study reports synthetic two-layer ReLU regression dynamics. It does not measure CIFAR classification error, spurious-local-minimum frequencies as teacher and student widths grow, depth degradation, initialization-dependent signal propagation or trainable depth, stability-threshold learning rates, or batch-normalization benefits. Its own results therefore test none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors identify quenching and activation under conventional scaling, a transition toward RF-like dynamics at larger widths, and more uniform neuron participation under mean-field scaling. They propose quenching and activation as an implicit-regularization mechanism. Section 4.1 explicitly reports exponential convergence of training error to zero. These are synthetic regression findings, and the transition criterion remains subjective and fuzzy.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses two-layer ReLU networks trained by GD on synthetic regression targets, with conventional or mean-field scaling; it does not use benchmark classification training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Behavior changes with width relative to sample size and input dimension, conventional versus mean-field scaling, and target-function structure. The authors describe the NN-like/RF-like transition region as fuzzy and the classification/generalization setting as outside this study.

fits_no_version.finding: For m = 2000, n = 200, d = 20, the authors report training squared loss converging exponentially to zero for the neural network and associated random-feature model while test error saturates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Highly over-parameterized two-layer synthetic regression can achieve zero training squared loss through GD while remaining close to fixed-feature dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: Under conventional scaling, the single-neuron regression experiments show an initial RF-like phase followed by sparse neuron activation; behavior changes with width relative to sample count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conventional two-layer ReLU regression training can transition from fixed-feature-like dynamics to sparse feature learning, depending on parameter regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Under mean-field scaling, almost all neurons move significantly and contribute in the single-neuron population experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mean-field scaling changes neuron participation relative to the sparse activation observed under conventional scaling.

record.problems: Synthetic regression targets rather than benchmark classification; several training-error outcomes are shown only in figures without exact values; no uncertainty estimates are reported for these numerical experiments; the authors call the NN-like/RF-like transition criterion subjective and say the transition is fuzzy.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted; several separate plotted training curves are figure-only, and the paper does not supply prose endpoints that would allow further separate numeric training-error rows.

untested.parts: Convolutional classification training on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, label corruption, and the specified model-size and training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies as teacher and student grow together, and their reduction with one or two extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, and deep plain or normalization-free residual training recipes.

Activation-matched signal/gradient preservation, training-speed and depth benefits, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization. Appendix A.1 compares qualitative dynamics under two outer-layer initialization scales without testing these effects.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, transient loss recovery, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed claim versions; this does not negate the explicitly reported regression convergence in R3–R4. No verdict labels apply. Figure 17's measure mismatch requires correction.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification, random or corrupted labels, and comparisons among model sizes, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, plain versus residual shortcuts, ImageNet/CIFAR classification, and special deep-network recipes.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and training depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature/sharpness, and loss recovery or divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons and its effect on accuracy speed or learning-rate tolerance.
